1.title: CDMP FUNDAMENTALS
1.text: Welcome to Module 10: Reference and Master Data. This is Chapter 10 of the DMBOK, and it's a high-weight chapter — around ten percent of the exam, roughly eleven questions. This is where we tackle the "golden record" and Master Data Management, or MDM, one of the most practically important disciplines in data management. The exam tests several precise distinctions here, so let's work through them carefully.

1.title: Module Overview & Learning Objectives
1.text: Here's our plan. You'll distinguish reference data, master data, and transactional data — a distinction the exam tests constantly. You'll learn the Gartner definition of MDM and the three goals. You'll work through Chisholm's six-layer reference data taxonomy. You'll understand entity resolution and the three matching workflows. You'll compare the three MDM architectures and the five implementation styles. And you'll recognize the golden record concept, governance, and metrics. Let's start with definitions.

1.title: Definitions & Goals
1.text: Let's define our two data types. Reference data is any data used to characterize or classify other data, or to relate data to information beyond the enterprise — things like codes and categories. Master data is data about business entities — customers, products, employees, locations — that provides context for transactions, and it represents the most critical shared data across the enterprise. For MDM itself, memorize the Gartner definition: a technology-enabled discipline in which business and IT work together to ensure uniformity, accuracy, stewardship, semantic consistency, and accountability for the enterprise's official shared master data assets. Note those five qualities. The three goals are: ensure access to accurate, complete, and consistent reference and master data; enable sharing across the enterprise; and reduce risk and cost through proper stewardship.

1.title: Reference vs. Master vs. Transactional
1.text: This three-way distinction is the single most tested concept in the chapter, so let's nail it with the three cards on screen and a concrete example. Reference data classifies or categorizes other data — think status codes, country codes, or a product code set. Master data is the core shared business entity — the customer, the product, the employee. And transactional data records a discrete business event at a point in time — a sales invoice, an order, a withdrawal. So when you see a sales invoice, that's transactional. The product code set it references is reference data. And the customer profile it points to is master data. The exam will give you a scenario like this and ask you to classify each piece. Practice that mapping until it's instant: event is transactional, entity is master, code set is reference.

1.title: Business Drivers
1.text: Why do organizations invest in reference and master data management? To reduce the inconsistency that comes from having multiple versions of critical data. To improve the data quality of customers, products, and other key entities. To support regulatory compliance. To enable better decision-making with consistent, accurate master data. To support data integration and interoperability. And to reduce redundancy and the cost of managing duplicated data. The most concrete, quantifiable benefit the exam likes to cite is the elimination of duplicate records — which directly reduces the cost of duplicate mailings and improves the accuracy of cross-sell targeting. That's the kind of measurable operational win that justifies an MDM business case.

1.title: Reference Data — Chisholm's 6-Layer Taxonomy
1.text: Malcolm Chisholm gives us a useful six-layer taxonomy for reference data, organized by where the data comes from. Layer one is internal reference data, created and maintained within the enterprise — like department codes or cost-center codes. Layer two is industry reference data, set by industry groups — like SIC codes or SWIFT codes. Layer three is national reference data, defined by national bodies — like state codes or zip codes. Layer four is international reference data, from international bodies — like ISO country codes and ISO currency codes. Layer five is third-party reference data, commercially available — like Dun and Bradstreet DUNS numbers. And layer six is reference data derived from other reference data, created by combining or transforming existing reference data. The progression runs from the most local to the most external, then derived.

1.title: Reference Data Standards & Sources
1.text: A practical rule for reference data: wherever a recognized external standard already exists, adopt it instead of inventing your own codes. The exam likes a few examples. ISO gives us 3166 for country codes and 4217 for currency codes. SIC and NAICS classify industries. SWIFT, or BIC, codes identify banks. Dun and Bradstreet's DUNS number is a third-party business identifier. And GS1 standards, like UPC and EAN, identify products. The key governance distinction is internal versus external: internal code sets you define and maintain yourself, while external standards you adopt and track — you follow their updates rather than changing them. So prefer external standards for interoperability, and map your internal codes to them through cross-references.

1.title: Reference Data Types & the ICD Example
1.text: Reference data also comes in types of increasing complexity. The simplest is a list — just enumerated values, like status codes of Active and Inactive. Next, cross-reference tables map values between two or more classification systems. Then taxonomies provide hierarchical classification. And most complex are ontologies, which are networks of concepts and relationships. Reference data is organized into domains — sets of values that classify or categorize. A great example the exam uses is medical diagnostic codes: ICD-9 has approximately thirteen thousand codes, while ICD-10 expanded dramatically to approximately sixty-eight thousand codes for greater specificity. So remember the type progression — lists, cross-reference, taxonomies, ontologies — and that ICD-10 has about sixty-eight thousand codes.

1.title: Managing Reference Data — Crosswalks & Repositories
1.text: Here's a problem reference data has to solve: different systems use different codes for the very same concept. One system stores gender as "M," another as "Male," a third as "1." Managing reference data means reconciling those — and the tool for that is the cross-reference table, or crosswalk, shown on screen. A crosswalk maps each system's codes to one shared, canonical set, so System A's "M" and System B's "Male" both resolve to a single canonical value like "MALE." And rather than scatter these code sets across spreadsheets, you keep them in a reference data repository — a single managed home that stores each canonical set along with its definitions, owners, and effective dates. So remember: a crosswalk maps between code sets, and the repository is the one managed place those sets live.

1.title: Master Data Domains
1.text: Master data represents the most important shared entities in the enterprise, providing context for transactional data, and it has to be consistent across multiple systems. The common master data domains are: party — which covers person, organization, customer, employee, and supplier; product or item; financial — accounts, cost centers, and general ledger codes; location — addresses and geography; asset; contract or policy; rule; and concept, like industry classifications. The two most common and most frequently managed domains are party and product — customer and product master data are where most MDM programs begin, because they're the entities that cause the most pain when they're inconsistent.

1.title: Customer & Product — The Most Common MDM Domains
1.text: Of all the master-data domains, two dominate in practice: party — especially customer — and product. Customer MDM aims to build a single, trusted customer-360 view, pulling together every interaction across channels. A key technique here is householding, which groups related individuals or accounts into one economic unit — a family, or in B2B, an organization with its hierarchy of subsidiaries. Product MDM, often called PIM, creates one consistent product definition across the catalog, the website, and the ERP, including categories and variants. These two domains tend to deliver the clearest return on investment: de-duplicated customers mean cheaper mailings and better cross-sell, and consistent products mean accurate catalogs and fewer order errors. For the exam, party and product are the most common master-data domains, and usually where an MDM program starts.

1.title: Master Data Hierarchies & Relationships
1.text: Master data is more than flat records — stewards also manage the hierarchies and relationships that connect entities. Think of organizational rollups, where an employee belongs to a team, which belongs to a division, which belongs to the company. Or product taxonomies, where a SKU rolls up to a category and a line. Or customer affiliations and households, grouping members of one economic group. A subtlety the exam may probe: ragged, or unbalanced, hierarchies have branches of different depths, and they have to be modeled explicitly rather than assumed uniform. And getting hierarchies right matters enormously, because a wrong rollup silently corrupts every report built on top of it. So remember: managing hierarchies and relationships, not just values, is a defining stewardship duty for reference and master data.

1.title: System of Record vs. System of Reference
1.text: Two terms the exam likes to contrast: system of record and system of reference. A system of record is the authoritative source where an attribute originates and is maintained — the place the data is truly mastered. A system of reference is a trusted, governed copy that consumers actually read from, fed by that system of record — the MDM hub distributing master data outward is a classic example. And here's the nuance: MDM governance defines the system of record per attribute, which means different attributes of the same customer might originate in different systems — the billing address from one, the credit rating from another. So lock in the distinction: system of record is where data is authoritatively maintained; system of reference is the trusted distribution copy that consumers read.

1.title: Entity Resolution & Matching
1.text: Entity resolution is the process of identifying, matching, and linking records that refer to the same real-world entity — figuring out that "Bob Smith" in one system and "Robert Smith" in another are the same person. There are two matching approaches. Deterministic, or rules-based, matching uses exact or near-exact matching rules; it gives high precision but requires clean data to work well. Probabilistic, or statistical, matching uses statistical weights to score the likelihood of a match, which lets it handle data inconsistencies that would defeat exact rules. There's also an efficiency technique called blocking, or candidate generation: you use a coarse key — like a phonetic key derived from a last name — to shrink the comparison space before running detailed match scoring, so you're not comparing every record against every other record. Deterministic is exact rules; probabilistic is statistical scoring.

1.title: The 3 Matching Workflows & the Golden Record
1.text: Once you can match records, there are three workflows for what to do with the matches. Duplicate identification finds records representing the same entity and marks the duplicates, without changing the source systems. Match and link identifies matches and links them to a golden record, but without physically consolidating them — the sources stay separate. And match and merge identifies matches and actually merges them into a single, consolidated golden record. That golden record — also called the best version of truth, exactly as the diagram on screen shows — is the authoritative, consolidated record created from the matched records. And survivorship rules determine which attribute values "win" and survive into the golden record when sources disagree. The key distinction for the exam: match-and-link keeps the sources separate, while match-and-merge consolidates them into one.

1.title: Building the Golden Record — Survivorship & Trust
1.text: Let's go deeper on how the golden record actually gets built, because it's derived, not typed in by hand. When two matched records disagree on a value, survivorship rules decide which one wins. The common rules: most recent, where the latest update wins; most complete, where a populated value beats a blank; source priority, where a ranked, trusted source wins; and most frequent, where the value that appears most often wins. To support these, each source carries a trust or confidence score that weights its values, and provenance metadata records exactly where each surviving value came from. So the golden record — the best version of truth — is assembled, attribute by attribute, by applying survivorship rules and source trust across all the matched records.

1.title: MDM Architecture Types (3)
1.text: There are three primary MDM sharing architectures, drawn side by side on screen, and the exam tests them directly. The registry, or index, architecture maintains an index of where master data lives in the source systems — it does not store the master data itself; it just links to the sources. This makes it minimally invasive, and the sources remain authoritative. The transaction hub is a central master data hub where all transactions go through the hub, which becomes the system of record. This gives the strongest data governance and a single point of control, but it's complex to implement. And the consolidated, or repository, architecture maintains a physical consolidated copy of the master data, synchronized periodically. It's better for analytics, but it isn't always real-time, so it may have latency. The shorthand: registry is index-only with no data moved, transaction hub is central control, and consolidated is a physical copy.

1.title: MDM Implementation Styles (5)
1.text: Closely related to the architectures are five implementation styles. Registry, as we covered, is the cross-reference index that doesn't alter the sources. Consolidation creates a physical merged copy. Coexistence allows multiple authoritative sources to coexist, kept synchronized between them — a hybrid approach. Transaction hub validates all transactions against the hub. And centralized makes one system the single source of truth for all consumers. Two exam scenarios to recognize: if you cannot modify the source systems — say, due to regulatory constraints — the right style is registry, because it only indexes. And if new records must route through the hub before being assigned an enterprise ID, that's the transaction hub style, with the hub as system of record.

1.title: MDM Hub Components
1.text: An MDM hub is built from several components, and the exam occasionally asks which component does what. The match and merge engine runs the matching algorithms and builds the golden records. The data stewardship interface is where suspected duplicate records are presented to human reviewers for resolution decisions — so when a match is uncertain, a human steward decides. The services layer, or API gateway, exposes standardized interfaces so that consuming applications can retrieve and update master data without needing to know the hub's internal data model — it abstracts the internals. And the workflow engine orchestrates the stewardship tasks and approvals. The two most testable: the stewardship interface is where humans resolve uncertain matches, and the services layer hides the hub's internal structure from consumers.

1.title: MDM Depends on Data Quality & Integration
1.text: One big-picture point before we move to governance: MDM is never a standalone tool — it stands on three other disciplines you've already studied. First, entity resolution, the deterministic and probabilistic matching that finds records referring to the same entity. Second, data quality — profiling, cleansing, and especially standardization — because records can only match if they've first been cleaned and put into a common form. The exam framing is blunt: you cannot master dirty data. And third, data integration, the ETL or ELT that loads and synchronizes master data across systems. All three operate under data governance, which sets the stewardship, the rules, and the system of record. So the key dependency to remember: MDM depends on data quality — you standardize and cleanse before you match, or the matching simply fails.

1.title: Governance & Reference Data Change Management
1.text: Governance is critical for this knowledge area. Stewardship responsibilities include defining and managing the reference data domains, resolving conflicts between classification schemes, approving changes to reference data values, and managing hierarchies and relationships. Reference data change management has a specific exam angle: changes to reference data values must be handled as formal changes, historical values must be preserved for backward compatibility, and you use effective-dated records to track value changes over time. For master data governance, you assign stewards per domain, define the system of record for each attribute, manage data quality rules, and monitor the matching rules and golden record creation. The point to remember: reference data changes are effective-dated and preserve history — you never just overwrite an old code.

1.title: Activities, Tools & Metrics
1.text: Let's cover activities, tools, and metrics together. The five activities are: define the reference data strategy, define the MDM strategy, identify reference data sources, establish reference data governance, and implement the MDM solution. The tools include entity resolution engines that do deterministic and probabilistic matching, data quality tools for profiling and cleansing, data integration tools for loading master data, and workflow tools for stewardship approvals. And the metrics fall into six categories: completeness, coverage, quality, matching, timeliness, and usage. Two worth noting: matching metrics use precision and recall — the same retrieval concepts from the last chapter — and coverage measures the percentage of enterprise entities that actually have master records. Six metric categories, with matching measured by precision and recall.

1.title: Key Numbers & Quick Facts (Cheat Sheet)
1.text: Let's consolidate. Reference data classifies, master data is the entity, transactional data is the event. The MDM definition is Gartner's, emphasizing uniformity, accuracy, stewardship, and semantic consistency. Chisholm gives six reference data layers. Reference data types run from lists to cross-reference tables to taxonomies to ontologies. ICD-9 has about thirteen thousand codes, ICD-10 about sixty-eight thousand. The two matching approaches are deterministic and probabilistic. The three matching workflows are duplicate identification, match-and-link, and match-and-merge. The three architectures are registry, transaction hub, and consolidated, and there are five implementation styles. The golden record is the authoritative consolidated record. And there are six metric categories. Drill these.

1.title: Common Exam Traps
1.text: Here are the traps. First, a sales invoice is transactional data, not master data — the customer and product it references are the master and reference data. Second, the registry MDM architecture does not store the master data; it stores only an index pointing to the sources. Third, match-and-link does not merge records — link keeps the sources separate, while merge consolidates them. Fourth, deterministic matching needs clean data and uses exact rules; it's probabilistic matching that handles messy, inconsistent data. And fifth, reference data is not the same as master data — reference classifies, master is the entity itself. One more shortcut: when a scenario says you can't touch the source systems, the MDM answer is almost always registry.

1.title: Module Summary
1.text: Let's wrap up. Reference data classifies other data, master data is the core shared entity, and transactional data is the event — that three-way distinction is everything in this chapter. MDM, by Gartner's definition, ensures uniformity, accuracy, stewardship, and semantic consistency, and Chisholm gives you six reference data layers. Entity resolution, whether deterministic or probabilistic, feeds three matching workflows that build the golden record. There are three architectures — registry as an index, transaction hub for central control, and consolidated as a physical copy — plus five implementation styles. You govern with effective-dated reference changes and per-attribute systems of record, and you measure across six categories. That's Chapter 10.

1.title: Let's Test Your Knowledge
1.text: Time for five practice questions on reference and master data. These focus on classifying the data types and choosing the right MDM architecture for a given scenario. Read each carefully, decide on your answer, and then reveal the solution. Here we go.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one: classify the invoice, the SKU code set, and the customer profile. The answer is B — the invoice is transactional because it records an event, the SKU code set is reference data because it classifies products, and the customer profile is master data because it's a core shared entity. This three-way mapping is the chapter's signature test.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two: a firm must reconcile customer data across twelve systems but cannot modify any source's write path. Which implementation style? The answer is B — registry, because it creates a cross-reference index without altering the source records. Coexistence, transaction hub, and centralized all write to or intercept the sources, which is forbidden here.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three: new customer records from any channel route through the MDM hub before getting an enterprise ID, and operational systems are no longer authoritative. Which style? The answer is B — transaction hub, where the hub is the system of record and every new record flows through it. Registry only indexes; coexistence keeps multiple authoritative sources. Two more on the next slide.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four: the most concrete operational benefit for an MDM business case? The answer is C — eliminating redundant customer records, which reduces duplicate-mailing costs and improves cross-sell targeting accuracy. That's a measurable, MDM-specific win. The other options — converting unstructured data, replacing all legacy systems, or fewer committee meetings — aren't core MDM benefits. Question five: generating a phonetic key from last names to shrink the comparison space before detailed scoring. What's that technique called? The answer is D — blocking, also called candidate generation. By grouping records under a coarse key, you only compare plausible candidates in detail, dramatically reducing the number of comparisons. Threshold calibration and survivorship come later in the match process, and normalization is data cleanup. That completes Module 10. Next up is Module 11, Data Warehousing and Business Intelligence — another high-weight chapter at around ten percent. I'll see you there.
